item.title: The Daily Star – ‘Hollywood, Ending’ and the pressures of fame
item.description:
“You exchange pieces of yourself for celebrity. Celebrity keeps you working, keeps you paid. Keeps me paid, too,” a reporter tells Kai Laramie in Hollywood, Ending.

“Except once I’ve traded those little pieces of myself, I can’t get them back. They’re not mine anymore,” he replies.

These lines capture the bargain at the centre of John Green’s first novel in nine years and his debut in adult fiction. Two actors in their early 20s discover how easily the pursuit of recognition can blur the line between sharing their lives and losing control of their stories. Juniper Castillo, a former Nickelodeon child star, and Kai, a newcomer to film, are cast opposite Marvel superstar Matthew Malone in an art-house Andy Warhol biopic. When 92 per cent of test-screening respondents rate the film in the top two categories, it has a real chance of finding an audience. Its cast must help make that happen. What interests Green is who gets to write the self that fame produces.

Told from the first-person perspectives of Juniper and Kai, the novel unfolds in four parts, following them from the filming of the biopic through its promotional rollout, premiere and aftermath. Warhol is a fitting subject for the biopic. His fascination with celebrity and images speaks to the novel’s interest in the gap between public identity and private life. Kai and Juniper must perform their roles on screen. They must also perform themselves.

The studio sees a possible romance between the two as another way to sell the film, encouraging speculation faster than either can work out what they feel off camera. Carefully planned social media posts help build a “will they, won’t they” narrative. The publicists who tell them to lean into the chemistry and give fans something to talk about see it as simply part of the job. Even affection becomes material.

Both protagonists have histories of childhood abuse. Kai finds the intrusion that comes with growing attention difficult to navigate. He refers to what happened to him only as “it.” When details of his past leak, he is hailed as a heroic survivor. The studio embraces that image and folds it into the film’s publicity.

Kai sits in windowless conference rooms as a new reporter arrives every seven minutes. They tell him, “You have been very public about this,” as though the fact that people know about his past means he chose to tell them. These encounters show how consent can be quietly distorted: a person is pressured into speaking, then treated as though speaking was always their decision.

The junket chapters become a run of talking points: “Matthew is a legend,” “I love Juniper” and “victims have nothing to be ashamed of.” The phrases are repeated until Kai recognises that, although he believes what he is saying, having to say it so often has begun to feel like a betrayal. The form enacts the theme: sincere words, emptied by repetition, become product. Kai grows increasingly uncomfortable with the idea that other people feel entitled to his story and can decide what it means.

Juniper has grown up in the industry and knows how to work within its demands. She has gone public with her story, handles interviews well and is ambitious and strategic about her image. She also understands the cost. “You don’t have to be an actor for the world to pound away at you, to render you two-dimensional, to villainize or heroize, or do both at once,” she says. “But if you’re an actor, everyone gets a ticket to the show.” The line applies to Kai too. He becomes a figure for other people’s purposes, one they can build up or tear down as they choose. The public feels entitled to watch and judge; the person in the spotlight has little say in the version of themselves that emerges.

We do not need to be movie stars today to feel the pressure to curate our lives online or to wonder how much of ourselves to share. We are conscious of which parts to reveal, which to keep private and how others might respond. The stakes are different in Hollywood, but the desire to have some say in how we are seen is familiar.

Green does not suggest that publicity or self-disclosure is always harmful. Openness can bring connection and meaning. His concern is with an industry that blurs the boundary between private life and publicity, turning personal experiences into commodities and privacy into something people are expected to surrender.

What gets taken is the freedom to be ambiguous: to have a feeling, a past or a self that has not yet become a story. The novel is at its best when it observes rather than resolves, and its observations are the reason to read it.

Shababa Iqbal is a journalist with a love for entertainment, fashion, lifestyle, and books, and a particular interest in youth-focused stories. Reach her at [email protected].

item.title: The Daily Star – The people we leave to drown
item.description:
I once helped a student from Madaripur prepare for his IELTS exam. For many youths in his region, owing to a lack of quality education and viable economic opportunities, there is only one goal in life: to go to Italy. My student was one of the lucky ones, to have the luxury of good education, prepare for an exam, and secure university admission as a legitimate pathway. Most of his friends, however, had already gone to Italy by “game.” I am not sure of the etymology of this word, certainly it’s not a simple loan and it has gone through a little semantic change, but “game” here refers to the perilous act of crossing the Mediterranean from the coast of Libya in a small dinghy or rickety boat. It is a gamble with the highest possible stakes, that thousands of youths take, so they could have a better future for themselves and their family.

This gamble turns into a tragedy for hundreds every year, if not more. Just last year, a boat carrying 56 people that had set sail from the Libyan coast capsized in the Mediterranean. When the bodies washed ashore, it was discovered that at least 10 of the 23 deceased were young men from the Rajoir Upazila of Madaripur. Families who had taken out crippling loans, sometimes as much as 20 lakh taka, to pay dalals were left with both an immense debt and also the unbearable grief of identifying their sons from photos of lifeless bodies circulating on mobile phones. This was not an isolated incident; it is a rather familiar story. It is one of the deadliest migration paths in the world, and for nearly a decade, a significant percentage of those risking it have been Bangladeshis.

This familiar story of human tragedy and systemic failure is the subject of Vincent Delecroix’s novel Small Boat. Brilliantly translated from the French by Helen Stevenson, the novel reconstructs a similar and real-life event, on the cold waters of the English Channel where 29 migrants try to cross the Channel and their small boat fails them as they relay their last urgent message of plea before death. No one comes to help them. Not that the authorities don’t know—they know—but the French say you’re in English water and the English say the French rescue vessel is near, and amidst this, 27 out of the 29 people die.

Shortlisted for the International Booker Prize of that year, Small Boat is a scathing critique of this animalistic apathy towards migrants. The novel is structured in three parts. The first and the last being narrated by a French coast guard operator whose sheer apathy led to the chilling death of 27 people, even though they could have and should have been saved. The second part of the novel is an omniscient third person narration and it reads like a shuddering horror story. 

Small Boat barely flounders, the two parts narrated by the French coast guard operator are a masterclass in sustained, claustrophobic psychological horror. Delecroix traps the reader inside the narrator’s mind, forcing us to listen to a relentless stream-of-consciousness that is chilling in its horrifying precision. Through her, we witness the process of dehumanisation: the migrants are reduced to voices on a radio, dots on a screen, a recurring annoyance in a long night’s shift. Her justifications, her professional detachment, and her blame-shifting arguments are presented with a terrifyingly plausible logic that builds a fortress of indifference around the tragedy. 

The true horror of the novel lies in this plausibility; it is the banality of apathy, where protocol and procedure become excuses for utter moral failure. While the book’s central section depicts the raw, physical terror of the sinking, these framing narratives too deliver lasting shock, revealing the cold, bureaucratic heart that allows the horror to happen in the first place. 

Bookended by these sections of chilling self-justification is the novel’s harrowing core. The narrative voice shifts to a stark, omniscient third-person that plunges the reader directly into the freezing water with the migrants. Here, the abstract “incident” becomes a visceral, moment-by-moment ordeal. Delecroix strips away all artifice, describing the sudden brutal shock of cold as the first person falls in, the false hope of a passing cargo ship whose searchlight “swept over them, but never fixed on one,” and their agonisingly slow surrender to their fate. 

The prose is unflinching, its power lying in its quiet, observational horror. It transforms the operator’s clinical detachment into an abject moral crime, forcing the reader to bear witness to the human suffering she chose to ignore. The final moments are detailed as a creeping, quiet dissolution: “There was a ringing in their ears and a kind of continuous stupor overcame them, an irresistible lethargy, which they mistook for calm and the subterranean, indestructible continuity of the vegetative state. In fact they were dying.”

In the early 19th century Paris, Théodore Géricault’s painting “The Raft of the Medusa” delivered a shock. It depicted the real-life survivors of a shipwreck, abandoned by their incompetent captain and the authorities, and in doing so, it indicated the moral bankruptcy of the state. Vincent Delecroix has given us the 21st century literary equivalent of that painting. While Géricault depicted the raw, physical agony of the abandoned, Delecroix goes one step further: he forces us to look through the eyes of the person who saw it all, could save them all, but chose not to do so. Small Boat is a masterpiece of perspective, a novel that understands that the ultimate tragedy goes far beyond the tragedy of the drowning ‘incident’, and it is the cold, calculated indifference that watches everything happen from a safe and comfortable shore: the indifference of all of us. We are all complicit.

Najmus Sakib studies Linguistics at the University of Dhaka. Reach him at [email protected].

item.title: The Daily Star – Ahmed Sofa and Albert Camus: Two intellectuals against the plague of society
item.description:
On the surface, the life and literary work of the iconoclastic intellectual from Bangladesh, Ahmed Sofa, and the timeless novel The Plague (1947) by French existentialist philosopher Albert Camus seem to be born of two widely divergent geographical and political environments. One was written in the setting of the post-World War II European disillusionment, fascism and existential fears, and the other, a post-colonial Bangladesh, Liberation War and political and social decay. But, a close examination of the theoretical undergrowth and implicit philosophies of their work shows a remarkable spiritual and philosophical unity between the thinkers of these two worlds. Their thought is humanistic existentialist, an uncompromising combat against the ‘plague’ of social degradation, and the dispassionate moral obligation of the intellectual.

Camus’s philosophy was rooted in the idea of the Absurd, or the meaninglessness inherent in life. Plague is a sudden outbreak of an epidemic in the Algerian city of Oran that is not just a disease but a deep metaphor for an irrational devastation thrown at the life of humankind. This plague represents fascism which is laying siege to human freedom. This “absurdity” is very much there in the life and literature of Ahmed Sofa, but not in the European sense, rather as a third-world political absurdity. Alatachakra (1985) or Gabhi Bittanto (1995) show us a society which is struck by a moral and intellectual epidemic in Sofa’s novels. If the spirit of the Liberation War is plundered in the case of independent Bangladesh and if intellectuals turn into scavengers of power, that reality of the society turns as besieged and senseless as Camus’s Oran. Like Camus, who celebrated man’s futile but heroic struggle against The Plague, Sofa’s essay “Buddhibrittir Natun Binnash” was his personal and philosophical stand against the rot of institutions and The Plague.

In Camus’ novel, The Plague is a sinister entity that infects all, and for which there is no way out. The people of Oran first try to ignore the epidemic, then panic, and finally rebel against it. Sofa’s “plague” is the mental subservientness, the lack of backbone and political opportunism of Bengali society as seen in the literature. Sofa’s characterisation of high-level corruption and sycophancy in the university in Gabhi Bittanto is a mirror image of a horrendous social scourge. The dirty political politics of everyone from the vice-chancellor to the teachers, played around an ox, are just as harmful as Camus’ metaphorical epidemic. In Sofa’s novel, The Plague wipes out the intellect and conscience of a nation while in Camus’ book, plague kills the human body. Both authors have shown that a plague shatters masks, revealing the deepest selfishness of humanity and its ability to make the greatest of sacrifices and show the greatest empathy.

The Plague’s main character, Dr. Bernard Rieux, is not a typical hero. He has no faith in God, and he doesn’t utter political dogma. He’s just doing what doctors do. In one of the famous dialogues in the novel Dr. Rieux remarks that The Plague offers no heroism, it is a matter of common decency. To him decency is nothing more than doing his job. The closest portrait of Dr. Rieux can be seen in Ahmed Sofa’s life and view of the writer. All of the time, Sofa was far away from the halls of power. To him, the job of an intellectual was the same as Dr. Rieux’s: When a society has a disease, tell the truth and cure them. Like Dr. Rieux’s refusal of performative heroism, sofa’s absolute disdain for state awards, institutional recognition or media fanfare. During the great Liberation War of 1971, he used his pen, he came out to the streets to fight against autocracy in this newly formed country and he inspired young writers, all in the name of conscience, in the name of his ‘decency’. Like Dr. Rieux, Sofa never gave up in the struggle against The Plague of political and cultural epidemics in Bangladesh.

The worst afflictions of the citizens of Oran in the time of plague was the agony of exile: a besieged city, isolated from their dear ones. Ahmed Sofa’s life was also a story of great isolation intellectually. He was an optimist and lived out his life honestly and without compromise, and this brought him into conflict with the opportunist society of his day. The culmination of this loneliness is in his Pushpa Brikkha Ebong Bihanga Puran (1996). Like Camus’ second characters, who find temporary solace by swimming in the sea to escape the terror of The Plague, Sofa, disillusioned with humanity, finds a refuge in flowers, vines and birds. His keen interest in plants and animal life on his roof wasn’t just a nature-loving pastime, it was a way to make sense of the world in an absurd, meaningless earth. Humanity is destroyed in the process and although society crumbles, nature is the last place one can turn. Sofa’s botanical and avian mythos is a quiet celebration of the very same philosophy as Camus’ philosophy, the joy of living amongst the void.

The famous words of Camus were “I rebel; therefore we exist.” The Plague is about how Dr. Rieux, Tarrou and Rambert transcend individual isolation to create a community, the sanitary squads. They know The Plague may never end; giving up without a fight is not human nature. In the life and in the works of Ahmed Sofa is this very story of a collective resistance. He did not write just for himself. The reverence he displays towards Abdur Razzaq in Jadyapi Amar Guru (1998) is an intellectual journey in search of a nation. Sofa felt that such a social evil or corruption could only be fought with a mass mental reawakening. He was the core of that opposition. Every time the country was in trouble—in military autocracy, or communal riots, or cultural imperialism, Sofa was in the front with his own ‘sanitary squad’: his pen and his young disciples. Sofa, like Camus’s characters in The Plague, struggled to preserve the dignity of the human person through his writings, and the dignity of the Bengali people through the struggle.

Stylistically the two are quite similar. The novel that Camus wrote is like a diary or a journalistic report; it’s dispassionate, like nothing is happening, yet it’s very passionate, burning under the surface. He didn’t embellish the terror of the epidemic with frills. The prose of Ahmed Sofa is also plain, pointed and taut. His essays lack any pretence, his novels any mawkish sentiment. In Alatachakra, the raw depiction of the refugee camps is without imagination, and without the bias of any dissection but that of the hard reality. As Camus, Sofa felt it was necessary to present the truth in its most bare and natural state.

On the last page of The Plague, Dr. Rieux reminds us that plague bacillus never really dies: it lurks for years in furniture and linens, awaiting the day it might once more rouse the rats of a happy city to bring a message of death. Similarly, through his literature Ahmed Sofa warned us. He continually pointed out the germs of fascism, bigotry, and sycophancy lurking in the crevices of our society. Whatever their differences in structure, both Camus and Sofa were indomitable architects of human existence, who, in the face of epic plagues, taught us to fight with common decency.

Md. Shihab Uddin is an independent researcher and an undergraduate student of Folklore and Social Development Studies at the University of Rajshahi. He may be contacted at [email protected].

Sofa felt that such a social evil or corruption could only be fought with a mass mental reawakening. He was the core of that opposition. Every time the country was in trouble—in military autocracy, or communal riots, or cultural imperialism, Sofa was in the front with his own ‘sanitary squad’: his pen and his young disciples. Sofa, like Camus’s characters in The Plague, struggled to preserve the dignity of the human person through his writings, and the dignity of the Bengali people through the struggle.

Stylistically the two are quite similar. The novel that Camus wrote is like a diary or a journalistic report; it’s dispassionate, like nothing is happening, yet it’s very passionate, burning under the surface. He didn’t embellish the terror of the epidemic with frills. The prose of Ahmed Sofa is also plain, pointed and taut. His essays lack any pretence, his novels any mawkish sentiment. In Alatachakra, the raw depiction of the refugee camps is without imagination, and without the bias of any dissection but that of the hard reality. As Camus, Sofa felt it was necessary to present the truth in its most bare and natural state.

On the last page of The Plague, Dr. Rieux reminds us that plague bacillus never really dies: it lurks for years in furniture and linens, awaiting the day it might once more rouse the rats of a happy city to bring a message of death. Similarly, through his literature Ahmed Sofa warned us. He continually pointed out the germs of fascism, bigotry, and sycophancy lurking in the crevices of our society. item.title: The Daily Star – Rage
item.description:
And one day—
When i pick my pen again,
All i have is rage 
Scratched on pages
Lines cut like bleeding wounds being cut twice
The sort of rage where my eyes burn
into a silent pain,
gradually radiating to my lower jaw
I clench so deep that I fail to realise 
there’s a circular trace of teeth on my hand 
Clear and red yet comforting in a way
my heart starts pounding to the physical pain
And my lungs? 
Flaring for air; yet prefers to live without it
I could think of a thousand different ways to hurt myself 
Just a visual representation of how love screwed up my mind 
I have rage to the point 
I could burn pages but not lives
I could complain to god but never let my prayers be the cause of your demise 
I could wish for you to live with the burden of regrets; alive but dead inside
And when memories rewind,
I fuel my rage with the poems I write

item.title: The Daily Star – Beyond the pond
item.description:
I sat by the pond after a long hiatus.
Just then, a butterfly drifted away,
slightly touching the water’s surface.
Like my transient youth,
a woodpecker took wing,
for it had to peck at wood
and drink its share of musky water.
A few ducks circled round and round,
in an attempt to create something
more sublime than the dictates of the food chain.
I turned to the child beside me.
“Look, there’s no world beyond the pond.”
The child laughed.
In its laughter live on
my ancestry,
my lineage.
 

Dr Shiblee Shahed is a public health specialist, essayist, poet, and translator. His debut poetry collection was published in 2013 by Shuddhashar Publications. His poems and articles have appeared in numerous national and international outlets. He is a regular contributor to The Daily Star.

item.title: The Daily Star – Humayun Ahmed's people in today's Dhaka
item.description:
I am sitting in a café in Banani when I see a group of teenagers scroll past a photograph of Humayun Ahmed. One of them shrugs. “His stories are old,” they say. “They don't resonate anymore.” I do not argue. But the sentence stays with me. A whole world—Himu's barefoot walks, Misir Ali's quiet logic, Baker Bhai's stubborn justice—is being politely shown out of the room.

Humayun Ahmed's world is my sanctuary. It is where I go when Dhaka becomes too loud. But the sanctuary feels far away. Everyone around me is optimising something: Careers. Side hustles. Online presence. The people Humayun Ahmed wrote about, the ones who refuse to optimise, seem like ghosts.

So let us imagine them. Not as relics in a book, but as people still living here. Himu walking through the traffic of Mohakhali. Misir Ali reading by the window in Aziz Super Market. Baker Bhai pouring tea at Kamalapur. It is Humayun Ahmed’s birthday soon, and this is my small attempt to bring them back into the room.

Himu still wears the yellow panjabi. It is faded now, thin from decades of humidity. It has no pockets. He walks barefoot along the broken footpaths, potholes, past the glass buildings of Motijheel. Due to global warming even in November, the footpaths are heated, it burns his feet. Rickshaws are battery-powered now. Tea stalls accept bKash. Young men who once would have stopped to listen to his strange, anti-logical pronouncements now hunch over their phones, scrolling through job listings. Himu has not changed. He has no job, no fixed address, no source of income. People ask him, with pity and irritation, “Himu bhai, don't you need a plan? A LinkedIn profile?” He laughs—that infuriating, detached laugh—and says he is still a beggar. But a beggar of a different kind. He begs for people to look up from their screens. To notice the rickshaw puller’s cracked hands. The tea-stall boy's tired smile. In a Dhaka obsessed with hustle, Himu remains the city's most radical refusal. He has stepped outside the script, without guilt and without a manifesto.

Rupa lives in Banani now, but she is no longer waiting. She runs an NGO for street children and navigates the city's traffic in an air-conditioned car. Her blue saree has been traded for a practical cotton salwar kameez. She speaks the language of donors and spreadsheets. She quantifies compassion in quarterly reports. But sometimes, on a Thursday afternoon, she leaves the office early. She takes a rickshaw to Ramna Park. She does not call Himu. The landlines do not exist anymore. She knows he is somewhere, walking, and that is enough. 

Misir Ali is harder to find. He has retired from teaching. The psychology department at the University of Dhaka felt too loud, too full of students who wanted answers rather than questions. He lives in a small flat near Aziz Super Market. Books surround him, and the faint smell of old paper. His health is as fragile as ever. The thin face. The thick glasses. The untidy beard that has turned white.

He does not accept money for solving mysteries. He still does not believe in the paranormal. But he has been called more than once to investigate a “haunted” Facebook page or a viral video of a jinn in a Mirpur basement. He declines most cases. “The real mystery,” he tells a young journalist who tracks him down for a birthday feature, “is not whether the ghost is real. It is why so many people need it to be.” He spends his evenings listening to an old transistor radio. A student once brings him an AI-generated "psychological profile” that claims to diagnose his personality from his Facebook posts. Misir Ali reads it three times, then he sets it aside. “A machine can catalogue my habits,” he says, "it cannot understand why I keep a diary called Unsolved.”

Baker Bhai is not dead. That is the rumour, anyway. The hangman's rope broke. Or the file was lost. Or the government decided that a dead folk hero was more dangerous than a living one. He is an old man now. He runs a tea stall near the Kamalapur railway station. The motorcycle gang is gone. But Baker Bhai still patrols the platform at night. He is not a gangster anymore. He is a self-appointed guardian of the tired and the lost. The city has CCTV cameras on every corner. But they do not see what Baker Bhai sees. They record, but they do not intervene.

Muna visits him sometimes. She is a widow now, her hair streaked with grey. She sits beside him in silence, watching the trains come and go. She manages a branch of a microfinance bank with quiet competence. But here, on the platform, she is simply Muna. And he is simply Baker Bhai. The city has forgotten the night thousands marched for him. He is still waiting, in his own way, for a world where justice does not require a martyr.

Ranu was the 17-year-old protagonist of Debi. She heard voices, predicted events she should not have known, and was studied by Misir Ali himself. She is in her ’50s now, living in Mohammadpur. Her flat is cluttered with photographs, medicine, and a small shrine in the corner. The voices have not left her. But they have changed. They are no longer whispers of a goddess or a spirit. They are notifications of a dozen apps. The ping of an email. The relentless chime of a news alert. 

The world of Ayomoy belongs to another century. It was the world of a declining zamindar family of the British Raj—the rural estate, the slow decay of an old order. But its characters have not vanished. They exist now as digital ghosts. Photographs on a genealogy website. Names in a family WhatsApp group. A great-grandson in Toronto who occasionally posts a scanned letter from the 1940s. The stories are no longer lived in the damp halls of a village mansion. They are archived, compressed, uploaded. The past has become data. And yet, something persists. The anxiety of decline. The fear of irrelevance. The struggle to hold on to dignity in a changing order.

And finally, there is Mr. Sobhan of Bohubrihi. He is the wealthy retired man of Dhanmondi who is always trying to solve social problems. He is always writing them down in his Google Keep notes. He is always failing because the problems he identifies have little to do with reality. He is in his ’80s now. He has discovered social media. He has a Facebook page dedicated to civic improvement. A Twitter account where he posts long, earnest threads about the state of the city. He is trolled relentlessly. He does not understand the trolling. He writes it down in his notebook. His wife Minu is still irritated with him. And his tenant, Anis—the widower who is good at giving advice—is still there, criticising every idea, shaking his head.

The problems have changed. Traffic. Pollution. The loneliness of a city where everyone is connected and no one is together. On Humayun Ahmed's birthday, someone places a single yellow flower on his grave at Nuhash Palli. Someone else still wears a blue saree to the Boi Mela. And somewhere, in a tea stall near Kamalapur, an old man raises a glass of cha to the sky and says, “Aaj Himu’r jonmodin. Kothao keu nei, tobuo shobai ache.”

Humayun Ahmed is not alive anymore. But his people are still here. They are stuck in traffic on the Airport Road, breathing air that tastes of dust and exhaust. They are anxious about job interviews, about rent, about the future. They are scrolling through their phones, ignoring the person beside them. But they are also still walking. Still questioning. Still refusing to be entirely defined by the city's relentless demands. They are the quiet argument against the loudest version of the present. They are the reminder that there are other ways to be alive. They always will be.

Nazmun Afrad Sheetol is navigating the world through words, pretending to be a literary diplomat. She can be reached at [email protected].

item.title: The Daily Star – A century of Abu Ishaque and the persistence of the human spirit
item.description:
A century after his birth on November 1, 1926, Abu Ishaque remains a paradox in Bangla literature: a writer of modest output and extraordinary literary reach. His three novels—Shurjo-Dighal Bari (1955), Padmar Palidwip (1986), and the detective novel Jaal (1988)—attest to a literary imagination less concerned with prolific production than with the moral anatomy of society. His achievement was not merely to portray the marginalised but to make those whom history routinely overlooks its most eloquent witnesses. His varied career in administration, policing, intelligence, and diplomacy sharpened his understanding of human psychology, particularly the hidden transactions of authority: how people command obedience, disguise self-interest, manipulate beliefs, and persuade the vulnerable that their suffering is inevitable.

Born in rural Bengal, Ishaque lived through the devastating famine of 1943, Partition, and the turbulence of Pakistan’s early decades. Yet his fiction seldom approaches these historical convulsions through political leaders or official narratives. Instead, he records their consequences in emptied kitchens, broken households, dispossessed cultivators, and women driven to the margins. For him, history is not simply what happens to a nation; it is what a nation permits to happen to its poorest citizens. His realism thus acquires a political dimension without surrendering its artistic independence.

In Shurjo-Dighal Bari, Ishaque’s finest achievement, Jaigun’s desperate search for food and shelter exposes the cruelty concealed within respectable social conventions. She must work to keep her children alive, but working outside the home invites condemnation for violating purdah. Society insists upon a woman’s modesty while denying her the material conditions of survival. The contradiction is devastating: the very activities through which Jaigun fulfils her maternal responsibilities become grounds for her public humiliation. Here, survival itself becomes an act of defiance.

The supposedly ill-omened house crystallises the novel’s larger argument. Its orientation is blamed for the family’s misfortunes, while the tangible sources of suffering—hunger, patriarchal violence, social hostility, and economic dependency—escape scrutiny. A fakir’s promise of supernatural protection converts fear into material profit. Superstition becomes more than mistaken belief; it functions as an ideological instrument that diverts attention from the structures of exploitation. The irony is unmistakable: the house is not cursed; the social order is diseased.

This relationship between belief and authority becomes particularly disturbing when religious functionaries collaborate with village headmen to enforce social obedience. Jaigun’s compulsory public repentance before her daughter’s wedding party demonstrates how religious rituals can be appropriated to discipline women whose poverty makes conformity impossible. Ishaque’s target, however, is not faith itself but its calculated manipulation. His fictional society reveals something akin to Antonio Gramsci’s concept of hegemony: domination sustained not merely through coercion but through the internalisation of beliefs that make inequality appear legitimate which is almost equal to self-subjugation of our women folk.

Ishaque nevertheless refuses the comforts of moral simplification. Jaigun is neither an immaculate heroine nor a self-conscious feminist. She resists injustice while occasionally reproducing the prejudices that sustain it, particularly in her attitudes towards marriage and the unequal social value assigned to sons and daughters. Her contradictions make her psychologically convincing. Emancipation in this novel is not an accomplished condition but an uneven struggle against the very assumptions that have shaped one’s consciousness. Jaigun’s rebellion is practical before it is philosophical.

Karim Bakhs, her brutal former husband, embodies another, equally compelling contradiction. Violent, possessive and deeply patriarchal, he initially appears an irredeemable villain. Yet his eventual sacrifice to protect Jaigun and her children transforms the reader’s understanding of his character. This final act cannot absolve his earlier cruelty; rather, it reveals an unexpected capacity for humanity. Where Jaigun demonstrates remarkable continuity of purpose, Karim Bakhs undergoes a profound moral transformation. Ishaque thus challenges simplistic distinctions between virtuous victims and wicked oppressors. The oppressed may internalise oppression, while even the oppressor may discover compassion.

This complexity extends to Ishaque’s representation of class. The poor are not invariably united, nor are they necessarily virtuous. Poverty produces suspicion, jealousy and rivalry as readily as solidarity. His village is consequently no pastoral sanctuary but a contested social world where landowners, religious intermediaries and local officials exercise power over those dependent upon them. Such realism reveals Ishaque’s socialist sympathies without reducing his fiction to ideological propaganda.

Padmar Palidwip extends this inquiry from domestic shelter to the unstable geography of Bengal’s riverine landscape. The Padma creates islands that erosion may subsequently erase; labour renders them productive, but power determines who possesses them. The house and the char thus become complementary symbols of precarious belonging. Nature provides land, human labour creates value, yet ownership remains governed by unequal social relationships. Both novels expose the distance between the elementary human need for security and the structures that perpetually frustrate it.

Ishaque’s historical imagination is equally perceptive. His portrayal of Partition exposes the limitations of political emancipation when economic and social hierarchies remain intact. National boundaries may change, governments may fall and new political identities may emerge, but the struggles of landless peasants and destitute women can persist almost unchanged. Political independence, his fiction suggests, cannot be equated with social liberation.

I encountered another dimension of Ishaque’s originality while translating Shurjo-Dighal Bari into English as The Ill-Omened House. His colloquial idioms, folk rhymes, religious expressions and socially differentiated voices presented formidable challenges. Their significance resides not merely in their literal meanings but in the cultural experiences they embody. To translate them mechanically would risk preserving information while extinguishing the vitality of the original.

More fundamentally, I confronted the relationship between grammatical tense and narrative time. Having travelled across different time zones, I had become conscious of the distinction between measurable time and its subjective experience. I therefore translated the first chapter predominantly in past tenses, since it establishes the narrative’s antecedents. From the second chapter onwards, I adopted the narrative present, shifting into the past whenever necessary. My intention was not grammatical experimentation for its own sake but to recreate the immediacy and uncertainty through which Ishaque’s characters experience their lives. Translation, I believe, demands fidelity not simply to words but to the movement of consciousness within a narrative.

At his centenary, Ishaque’s relevance remains undiminished. Gender discrimination, religious manipulation, economic dispossession and environmental insecurity continue to trouble our society. Yet his greatest achievement transcends these immediate concerns. He recognised that human beings are neither wholly noble nor irredeemably corrupt, and that resilience must never become an excuse for the injustice that makes it necessary.

Jaigun’s survival is heroic, but a society that demands heroism merely to stay alive stands morally condemned. The novel offers neither decisive victory nor comforting resolution. Its final movement affirms something more enduring: the unfinished struggle of human existence. Despite everything, they walk on.

She resists injustice while occasionally reproducing the prejudices that sustain it, particularly in her attitudes towards marriage and the unequal social value assigned to sons and daughters. Her contradictions make her psychologically convincing. Emancipation in this novel is not an accomplished condition but an uneven struggle against the very assumptions that have shaped one’s consciousness. Jaigun’s rebellion is practical before it is philosophical.

Karim Bakhs, her brutal former husband, embodies another, equally compelling contradiction. Violent, possessive and deeply patriarchal, he initially appears an irredeemable villain. Yet his eventual sacrifice to protect Jaigun and her children transforms the reader’s understanding of his character. This final act cannot absolve his earlier cruelty; rather, it reveals an unexpected capacity for humanity. Where Jaigun demonstrates remarkable continuity of purpose, Karim Bakhs undergoes a profound moral transformation. Ishaque thus challenges simplistic distinctions between virtuous victims and wicked oppressors. The oppressed may internalise oppression, while even the oppressor may discover compassion.

This complexity extends to Ishaque’s representation of class. The poor are not invariably united, nor are they necessarily virtuous. Poverty produces suspicion, jealousy and rivalry as readily as solidarity. His village is consequently no pastoral sanctuary but a contested social world where landowners, religious intermediaries and local officials exercise power over those dependent upon them. Such realism reveals Ishaque’s socialist sympathies without reducing his fiction to ideological propaganda.

Padmar Palidwip extends this inquiry from domestic shelter to the unstable geography of Bengal’s riverine landscape. The Padma creates islands that erosion may subsequently erase; labour renders them productive, but power determines who possesses them. The house and the char thus become complementary symbols of precarious belonging. Nature provides land, human labour creates value, yet ownership remains governed by unequal social relationships. Both novels expose the distance between the elementary human need for security and the structures that perpetually frustrate it.

Ishaque’s historical imagination is equally perceptive. His portrayal of Partition exposes the limitations of political emancipation when economic and social hierarchies remain intact. National boundaries may change, governments may fall and new political identities may emerge, but the struggles of landless peasants and destitute women can persist almost unchanged. Political independence, his fiction suggests, cannot be equated with social liberation.

I encountered another dimension of Ishaque’s originality while translating Shurjo-Dighal Bari into English as The Ill-Omened House. His colloquial idioms, folk rhymes, religious expressions and socially differentiated voices presented formidable challenges. Their significance resides not merely in their literal meanings but in the cultural experiences they embody. To translate them mechanically would risk preserving information while extinguishing the vitality of the original.

More fundamentally, I confronted the relationship between grammatical tense and narrative time. Having travelled across different time zones, I had become conscious of the distinction between measurable time and its subjective experience. I therefore translated the first chapter predominantly in past tenses, since it establishes the narrative’s antecedents. From the second chapter onwards, I adopted the narrative present, shifting into the past whenever necessary. My intention was not grammatical experimentation for its own sake but to recreate the immediacy and uncertainty through which Ishaque’s characters experience their lives. Translation, I believe, demands fidelity not simply to words but to the movement of consciousness within a narrative.

At his centenary, Ishaque’s relevance remains undiminished. Gender discrimination, religious manipulation, economic dispossession and environmental insecurity continue to trouble our society. Yet his greatest achievement transcends these immediate concerns. He recognised that human beings are neither wholly noble nor irredeemably corrupt, and that resilience must never become an excuse for the injustice that makes it necessary.

Jaigun’s survival is heroic, but a society that demands heroism merely to stay alive stands morally condemned. The novel offers neither decisive victory nor comforting resolution. Its final movement affirms something more enduring: the unfinished struggle of human existence. Despite everything, they walk on.

item.title: The Daily Star – ‘LISTEN’: Lending an ear to the stories of human trafficking survivors
item.description:
One of the only few things that a person can truly call their own is their body. But what happens when that very body, their very being is controlled by another, to be torn away from their identities, treated as commodity, bought and sold for consumption? That is what it means to be human trafficked, to be sold across borders, have one’s dignity stripped away from them, to be reduced to a commodity. 

Every year, hundreds of Bangladeshis aspire to rebuild their lives and secure a better future by crossing borders. Behind every statistic on human trafficking, behind every number, lies a story—one of a human life shaped by deception, tragedy, exploitation, and loss.

LISTEN: True Accounts of Those Who Survived Human Trafficking is a photobook that brings these stories to light. Launched by International Organization for Migration (IOM) Bangladesh, the photobook focuses exclusively on the diverse realities of human trafficking, documented through powerful visual storytelling and first-hand survivor narratives. First of its kind in Bangladesh, the publication places the voices and experiences of human trafficking survivors at the centre of the conversation.

This publication was developed with the support of the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA) under the project “A Comprehensive Counter-Trafficking Programme in Bangladesh”, implemented by IOM. 

Conceptualised by Pooja Bhalla and Soumin Shahrid of IOM Bangladesh, the photobook features the photographs by Soumin Shahrid. The documentation of the stories was done by Catherine Northing, Pooja Bhalla, Disha Sonata Faruque, Amal Biswas, Tarek Mahmud, Soumin Shahrid, and Fabiha Noshin, all from IOM Bangladesh. The publication was designed by Najnin Jahan Khan of Drik, which also handled its production in Bangladesh.

The book features the stories of 22 survivors of human trafficking. All of the stories in the book are narrated by the survivors themselves, including men and women of different ages, hailing from different corners of the country. Most of them come from humble backgrounds, many of whom had their lands swallowed by the river, some had been struggling with unemployment. Most, if not all of them, had been battling poverty, which compelled them to work as migrant workers in the first place. And it was during these vulnerable periods of their lives that they came across a dalal (referring to a middleman or intermediary) who is involved in recruitment processes linked to smuggling and trafficking. They play the role of a friend, a well-wisher, promising a dignified future and stable income. Sometimes it is one’s own family members. 

Most of the survivors featured in the publication were trafficked to the Middle East or SWANA (Southwest Asia and North Africa), while others were trafficked to India and other neighbouring countries. In the Middle East, the dalals betrayed the survivors and sold them to kafeels (sponsor or employer), taking away their passports and stealing their income, and trapping them in a life of physical, emotional and sexual torment and servitude. In its introduction, the photobook states that the kafeel is central to the Kafala system, a labour sponsorship framework in several Arab states that ties a worker’s legal status to the employer, which enables these employers to have complete control over the movement, employment and personal freedom of the workers—a total control over their lives.

On its cover photo, the book features the picture of a single ear. A woman’s ear, to be precise. Above the picture is the title, LISTEN, typed in red. The cover is meant to be striking, to catch the eyes of any onlooker, beckoning them to lend an ear. Beckoning them to listen to the voices of the victims of human trafficking, the ones who have seen the horrors and have returned to tell the tale. 

The book includes the stories of Latif, Mukta, Shabana, Rano, Salma, Masum, Robiul, Noor, Jannat, Ali, Putul, Farhana, Jhumur, Beli, Hashi, Nupur, among others. All of them had dreamt of building a better life, only to have their dignity and dreams trampled upon in the maws of trafficking. These stories however are not only about violence and exploitation the victims had faced abroad, but they also reveal yet another price of trafficking, the enduring trauma, silence and stigma that chase around the survivors long after their return. 

Each story is paired with a picture of the survivor, a translucent sheet in between. These sheets are not for mere decorative purposes. They carry quotes from the survivors, their agony inked in red. The photographs obscure the faces of the survivors for their protection, but the way in which it is done varies. The team behind the publication explained that every photographic manipulation, whether achieved through the camera or during post-processing, was entirely deliberate. The testimony of the survivor impacted all of it. 

“A person's face is their most defining feature. So, when trying to tell their story without showing it, we face a unique set of challenges. Overcoming them requires extensive research and a range of creative approaches,” said Soumin Shahrid, the photographer who co-conceptualised the publication.

Rano had one of the more horrifying stories of the book, who lost her uterus due to the horrific sexual and physical violence enacted upon her.  In the name of being employed as a domestic worker in the gulf, she was trafficked, starved, raped and beaten at the hands of four brothers. After somehow informing the police with the help of a hospital cleaner, Rano was rescued. Her battle was far from over, upon arrival at Bangladesh, she had to be taken to her hospital. Her uterus had to be removed. It didn’t stop there. Her husband stopped meeting her gaze and she was faced with judgement back home. Unable to bear it, at one point, she had tried taking pesticide to end her life. She survived that too. 

Shahrid said that when depicting Rano’s story, he had deliberately used a negative frame featuring a portrait of Rano in the middle of a colorful photo of a field. That frame was used to represent the societal stigma that the survivors face, and to reflect the loss of identity and the defacing nature of trauma, he had deliberately scratched out her face. 

When speaking to the team behind the publication, it was mentioned that the testimonies printed in this book are in fact, the most sanitised versions of these accounts of survival. The excruciating details in the unfiltered testimonies would confront readers with horrors that no work of fiction could come close to imagining.

There is a particular heartbreak evident in many of these stories, the one where the survivor is betrayed by a loved one. For some it is a family friend or a cousin that they grew up with, for some it is their own father. Most of the testimonies in this book are from women and girls, all of whom had endured horrific sexual violence. But their torment does not end at returning back home, upon returning, they are judged viciously, reduced to someone to gossip about. One of the survivors, Noor, was forced to take prostitution voluntarily simply because she was treated as though it was all that she was good for. Some were accepted, even supported by their partners in the pursuit of justice like Jannat, most were not. At times, these survivors were attacked by the traffickers even after they had been rescued. 

The final photo of the book shows a survivor holding an old photograph of himself from before he was trafficked, attempting to wipe it clean. The team shared that while showing the old photo, the survivor repeatedly lamented, “Look how vibrant I used to be before, now everything has been ruined!”

This book is not just about loss and sorrow, but also about resilience as all of the survivors in this photobook had survived the ordeal they had been through and were slowly building their lives once again with the help of IOM. These support include psychosocial support, lifeskills and financial literacy training, livelihood assistance, and community sensitisation provided under the project.

With that said, support systems for survivors of human trafficking need to be strengthened and made more responsive to their needs, including long term tailored psychosocial support for the survivors. This photobook serves as a stark reminder of the realities faced by thousands of migrant workers abroad, bringing to light personal accounts of how they were deceived, abused and had their humanity denied. And yet, they still stand up again.

Tiasha Idrak is drowning in a swamp of her own thoughts at the moment. She writes and daydreams, the latter is more applicable most of the time. She is still trying to come up with a proper author’s bio. Tell her to stop procrastinating at [email protected].

item.title: The Daily Star – Finding home, identity, and art in ‘Parsa’s Pithas’
item.description:
How do you stay connected to your own culture and roots while living thousands of miles away from home? This is the question at the heart of Sumaiya Matin’s debut children’s book Parsa’s Pithas. Set in Canada, the book tells the heartwarming story of a seven-year-old girl named Parsa who, through making pithas with her mother, is able to learn more about her Bangali roots and traditions while also gaining more confidence in her ability to express herself through her art.

The book opens with the young protagonist frustrated at her inability to draw the “perfect” sky. In dire need of a distraction, Parsa decides to take a break from her school art project to instead help her mother make nakshi pakon pithas for the Bangla New Year. However, as the two begin to make the pithas, Parsa’s frustration returns when she realises that she cannot make pithas as smoothly and intricately as her mother. First struggling to make the right consistency of dough, and then betrayed by the breaking of a toothpick, Parsa struggles with a question that every artist has asked themselves at least once —does art have to be perfect in order to be good?

For Parsa, the answer to this question is found in her mother’s stories about the Bangladeshi women who first made nakshi pakon pithas. Learning about the girls in Bangladesh who made art with whatever they had—rice flower, sticks, stones, and thorns of date palm trees—inspires Parsa to jump over the hurdle of perfectionism and focus her energy and creativity in expressing herself in her own unique way rather than trying to replicate what others are doing.

It is in this intertwining of cultural lessons with a story of a young girl persevering and learning not to give up that Parsa’s Pithas achieves immaculately what every good children’s book sets out to do—act as “mirrors, windows, and sliding glass doors” for children around the world.

First introduced by children’s literature scholar, Rudine Sims Bishop, the concept of “mirrors, windows, and sliding glass doors” is a metaphor for the different ways in which children can see themselves and the world around them in children’s books. Mirrors signify children seeing their own experiences reflected in the books they read, windows symbolise children learning about different cultures through books, and sliding glass doors refer to children using their imaginations to enter experiences that are different from their own. Bishop argues that all three of these reading experiences are essential to the development of a growing child. What makes Parsa’s Pithas so remarkable is that it is able to do all three of these things at the exact same time.

Written primarily with Bangladeshi diaspora children in mind, the book puts to pages an experience that is not often represented in books or media. Though there are an abundance of Bangladeshi children’s books with representation of Bangladeshi characters, we seldom see books made specifically for children who are learning to navigate their Bangladeshi roots and identity while living away from Bangladesh. Acting as a mirror, the story of Parsa and her mother keeping Bangali traditions alive by celebrating Bangla New Year all the way in Canada allows children of the Bangladeshi diaspora to finally see their own unique experiences and struggles be represented on paper.

Acting as a window, Parsa’s Pithas being a book that is written in English and available on the international market, offers many children, both in Bangladesh and outside, an insight into the Bangali culture and its traditions. The stories of Bangladeshi women told to Parsa by her mother in the book, combined with the vibrant and colourful illustrations by Nesba Yousef, act as the perfect introduction to Bangladeshi history. Furthermore, by framing the cultural lessons within the narrative of a young girl struggling with her artistic expression, the book is able to introduce Bangladeshi culture and values not as something that is unfamiliar and distant, but rather as something that everyone can learn from and incorporate into their own lives.

Lastly, it is in this invitation to participate, that the book shines the brightest. Going a step further than just introducing Bangladeshi culture to readers, with a full recipe for nakshi pakon pithas and an activities section, the book invites readers not only to learn, but fully immerse themselves in the culture they just read about.

It is here also that Matin’s message of embracing uniqueness over trying to replicate things perfectly comes in full clutch. For children in the diaspora, taking part in their culture may not always look the same as what it does for children living in Bangladesh. Many of them may be working with different tools, ingredients, and circumstances. However, as Parsa learns, just because something is different does not mean it is any less meaningful or beautiful in its own right. Afterall, sometimes to keep a culture alive is to be brave and resourceful enough to make it your own.

Shanjida Nowshin Chowdhury is a lecturer in the Department of English and Modern Languages at North South University.
